name: Aranmula Parthasarathy Temple
tagline: Ancient Krishna shrine, river processions and the Aranmula mirror tradition
summary: Historic Vishnu/Parthasarathy temple on the Pamba riverbank—famous for Valla Sadhya, boat processions, the Aranmula kannadi mirror and longstanding links with Kerala wedding customs.
description: Aranmula Parthasarathy Temple is an ancient Vishnu shrine (a Divya Desam) on the banks of the Pamba river in Aranmula, Pathanamthitta. The temple’s rituals and festivals—especially boat processions and the Valla Sadhya feast—shape local religious life.

The temple gives rise to several marriage-linked traditions: the handmade Aranmula kannadi (metal mirror) originates here and is one of the ashtamangalyam (eight auspicious items) used in traditional Kerala wedding entry rites. The temple also provides a mantap/venue for thalikettu-style temple weddings and daily marriage rites under temple administration.

Visitors interested in nuptial customs come for blessings, to see festival processions (Garudavahana, Pallivettam, palliyodam arrivals) and to learn about the Aranmula mirror craft and its role as a traditional wedding gift. Many families combine a temple wedding or post-wedding visit with a sightseeing stop at the mirror workshops and the Pamba ghats.

Practical arrangements (mantap booking, marriage documents, darshan rules) are run by the temple administration; details and local practice vary, so confirm timings and booking procedures with the temple office before planning a wedding or a ritual visit.
highlights: One of the 108 Divya Desams—historic Parthasarathy (Krishna as Arjuna’s charioteer).
Aranmula Kannadi (handmade metal mirror) — part of ashtamangalyam in Kerala weddings.
Valla Sadhya and palliyodam processions on the Pamba River during temple festivals.
Garudavahanam, Pallivetta and Arattu processions during the 10‑day Thiruvutsavam.
Temple mantap available for thalikettu-style weddings (advance booking required).

sections.heading: Background
body: Aranmula Parthasarathy Temple is a major Krishna shrine revered in the Nalayira Divya Prabandham and classed as a Divya Desam. Local tradition links the temple to the Pandava prince Arjuna; the site and its river ghats host rituals and processions that remain central to village life. (See Kerala Tourism and Wikipedia entries.)

The Aranmula kannadi mirror tradition is historically tied to the temple and the local metalwork craft. These mirrors receive special prominence in Kerala wedding customs as one of the eight auspicious items (ashtamangalyam) traditionally presented during the bride’s entry.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Attend festival processions and river ceremonies: the temple’s ten‑day Thiruvutsavam (Makaram month) features Kodiyettu, Garudavahanam, Pallivettam and the Arattu bath; the Aranmula Valla Sadhya (boatmen’s feast) and palliyodam arrivals on the Pamba are among the most distinctive ritual spectacles tied to the shrine.

Explore marriage links: visitors can learn why Aranmula kannadi figures in wedding ashtamangalyam, watch (or buy from) local mirror workshops, and observe how the temple’s rituals—annadana/feeding traditions, thulabaram and festival processions—interweave with community marriage practices.

For couples: the temple maintains a mantap/space for thalikettu-style marriages and performs temple marriage rites; many families also bring newlyweds (or visit the temple after a wedding) to receive deity blessings—confirm booking, required documents and any darshan/ritual restrictions in advance.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Timings and access: the temple is administered by the Travancore Devaswom Board; standard darshan windows are early morning and evening (check the current schedule before you travel). The Aranmula ghats and mirror workshops are walkable from the temple.

Marriage logistics: the temple offers a mantap and carries out thalikettu-style marriages; local temple‑info pages list required identity/age documents, a modest enrollment fee and that advance booking is necessary (online booking may not be available). Confirm registration and legal marriage registration procedures separately—temple rites do not replace civil registration.

Practicalities: if you plan a wedding or post-wedding visit, contact the temple office to reserve the mantap, confirm timings (many rites conduct early morning ceremonies), ask about photography/drone rules, and check whether the newlywed couple may receive immediate darshan or are required to follow a local tradition (some local guidance indicates darshan may be limited the same day).

latest.text: Kerala Tourism and state pages continue to highlight the Aranmula Valla Sadhya and the role of the Aranmula mirror in wedding traditions; the destination page remains the primary official tourism reference for recent visitor information.

Thiruvutsavam (10‑day annual festival) and related processions (Garudavahana, Pallivettam, Arattu) are listed for 2026 on local temple festival pages—these remain the main occasions when river processions and Valla Sadhya return in full ceremonial form.

visitorInfo.bestTime: October–March for pleasant weather; festival season (Makaram/Onam) for processions and Valla Sadhya.
visitorInfo.howToReach: Aranmula is on the Pamba river in Pathanamthitta district. Nearest railhead: Chengannur (≈10 km). Nearest airports: Trivandrum or Kochi; regular bus services connect Aranmula to nearby towns. From Chengannur or local bus stops walk to the Pamba ghats and temple.
etiquette: Confirm mantap booking, fees and document requirements with the temple office well before the wedding—some local pages state advance booking is required and online booking may not be available.
If visiting for festival processions or Valla Sadhya, arrive early and expect crowds at the ghats; dress respectfully and follow temple dress codes.
Buy or view Aranmula kannadi at authorised local workshops; the mirrors have a GI-backed tradition and make a traditional wedding gift—ask vendors about origin and certification.
For legal marriage registration, complete civil registration separately; temple rites are religious and may require supporting government documents (ID, age proof, witnesses).
